name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,331

entries.clue: Piece of cake, sandwiches etc eaten outside (6)

blocks.note: the idiom for an easy task, not a slice of sponge
a meal taken in the open air

annotation.surface: A spread of cake and sandwiches laid out for eating in the open air.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Piece of cake' reads as part of the menu, but it is the idiom for something easy, a sense PICNIC shares in 'it was no picnic'.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: the idiomatic easy task, as in 'no picnic', and the literal outdoor meal.

blocks.note: an informal word for a fizzy soft drink
an informal, mainly American word for dad

annotation.surface: Someone offering a drink to their father.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma makes 'Drink' look like an order addressed to a father; it is simply the first of two definitions.
annotation.definitionFit: Two informal senses: fizzy soft drink (from the sound of the cork) and a casual name for a father.

entries.clue: Political party on trial in debate (7)

blocks.note: Con = Conservative, the British party
a test = a trial

annotation.surface: A political party put on trial in the middle of a debate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Debate' looks like a noun, the setting of the trial, but it is the verb: to dispute a claim.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to contest an election result is to argue against it.

blocks.note: in = occupying (a place)
to nick = to steal, to take as your own

annotation.surface: Something improper about taking over a police station, a 'nick' in British slang.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nick' is British slang both for a police station and, as a verb, for stealing; the verb sense is the one used.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: behaviour that is unseemly offends against propriety, so it is not appropriate.

blocks.note: a dark beer, once favoured by market workers
someone who carries luggage for a living

annotation.surface: A container for carrying drinks.
annotation.walkthrough: The two words read as one noun phrase, like a bottle holder, but each is a separate definition.
annotation.definitionFit: The beer is said to be named after the London street porters who drank it, so both senses share a root.

indicatorNotes.Flying: letters sent flying are scattered through the air and land in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: Someone flying asks which plane is the right one to board.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flying' and 'flyer' sit at opposite ends and make the clue look like it is about aeroplanes; the flyer is a bird.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the oystercatcher is a black-and-white shore bird, and any bird is a flyer.

indicatorNotes.Ultimately: ultimately means in the end, so take the end of the word

blocks.note: last letter of vast
to range = to roam or wander

annotation.surface: A shop boasting a huge range of goods in stock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Range' looks like a noun, a selection of goods, but it is the verb meaning to wander.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: a trove, as in treasure trove, is a store of valuable things built up and kept.

blocks.note: people in a race
up = ahead, as in 'two goals up'

annotation.surface: A question about whether the leaders of a race are really the reserve side.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'second team' is playful: not a reserve side but the team that finishes second.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom read literally: whoever finishes second in a contest is the runner-up, so a team placed second qualifies.

entries.clue: A little shrimp, and another animal (5)

indicatorNotes.A little: only a little of the phrase is used, so the answer is a small piece of it

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of shrimp through and into another

annotation.surface: A small shrimp beside some other creature.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Another' makes the shrimp look like the first of two animals, but it only supplies letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the giant panda is a bear-like animal, and the surface's 'another' fits it beside the shrimp.

entries.clue: Instrument taking intro from ballad equally quickly (7)

indicatorNotes.intro from: the intro of a song is its opening, so the opening letter of ballad

blocks.note: first letter of ballad
as = equally, as in 'as tall'
soon = quickly, before long

annotation.surface: An instrument that picks up the tune from a ballad at the same speed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Equally quickly' is two pieces, AS and SOON, echoing the phrase 'as soon as you can'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the bassoon is a double-reed woodwind instrument.

indicatorNotes.reported: what is reported is spoken, so the clue works on how a word sounds

blocks.note: a boar is a male pig

annotation.surface: A dull outing where the pigs were the talking point.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Swine' reads as an insult for a person, but here it is simply the animal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a bore is anything so tedious it numbs the mind.

indicatorNotes.periodically: something done periodically recurs at regular intervals, so every other letter

blocks.note: v = versus, as in sports fixtures
the second and fourth letters of tiger

annotation.surface: A fight against a tiger.
annotation.walkthrough: Take the even letters of 'tiger', not the odd ones, or the answer will not fit.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to vie is to strive or compete against a rival.

blocks.note: the V sign made with two fingers
to signal = to point out or show

annotation.surface: A clear signal that someone has won.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clear' reads as an adjective describing the sign, but it is a verb: to clear someone's name.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: to vindicate is to clear someone of blame or suspicion.

blocks.note: per = by, as in 'per post'
grave = serious, harsh

annotation.surface: Mourners told not to linger by a graveside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grave' reads as a burial place but is the adjective meaning serious.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by paraphrase: to keep going in spite of difficulty is not to stop.

entries.clue: People in North America, one in a hundred (6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places one piece inside another, here the one inside the hundred

blocks.note: the initials of North America
a ton = a hundred, as in a hundred runs or miles per hour
Roman numeral one, placed inside TON

annotation.surface: One North American in every hundred belonging to some group.
annotation.walkthrough: 'People' is the definition in the singular sense, a people, as in 'the peoples of the world'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a people sharing a land, language or history is a nation.

indicatorNotes.playing: playing with something rearranges it, and it also suits the theatre surface

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

annotation.surface: A performer in a play wondering if the rest of the cast are much the same.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the fodder: people similar to a co-star are others in the same profession.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic hint, flagged by the question mark: a co-star is one of the cast, so people like them are performers too.

entries.clue: Indignation of king trapped during power cut (7)

indicatorNotes.trapped during: something trapped during an event is held inside it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: an outage = a failure of the power supply
R = rex, Latin for king; it goes after the third letter

annotation.surface: A monarch fuming at being stuck in a lift during a blackout.
annotation.walkthrough: The king is R, from Latin rex, as seen on British coins and postboxes.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: outrage is strong indignation at a wrong.

indicatorNotes.with some: taking only some of the following words means a piece of them

blocks.note: the last three letters of spoken and the first of traditions

annotation.surface: A region known for its oral traditions.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spoken' tempts a sound-alike, but the answer sits inside the words. Kent is a county in south-east England.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Kent is one of the counties of England.

entries.clue: Snare, net I wove with purpose (2,7)

indicatorNotes.wove: weaving threads twists them over and under into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: A trapper describing how they made a net with determination.
annotation.walkthrough: The snare and net keep the surface on trapping, so 'wove' looks like part of the story.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to do something in earnest is to do it seriously and with purpose.

indicatorNotes.for cooking: cooking mixes ingredients and changes them

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 5 letters

annotation.surface: A tree that grows cooking apples.
annotation.walkthrough: An apple for eating raw is the opposite of a cooking apple, so 'for cooking' pulls the wrong way.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: in Britain an apple grown to be eaten raw is an eater, as opposed to a cooker.

indicatorNotes.coming round: something coming round turns to face the other way, so read it backwards

blocks.note: a pit = a mine, as in a coal pit

annotation.surface: A forecast about a mine reopening.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mine' reads as the possessive, my prediction, but is the noun for a place dug for coal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from racing: a tip is a forecast of the likely winner.

entries.clue: Pull a trolley back in the midst of battle (7)

indicatorNotes.back: going back means travelling the other way, so the word is read right to left
indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the reversed trolley inside the letters from battle
indicatorNotes.the midst of: the midst of something is its middle, so the central letters of battle

blocks.note: as printed
the middle two of the six letters of battle
a cart = a trolley; reversed and put between the two Ts

annotation.surface: Someone hauling a trolley backwards through the thick of a fight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pull' is a verb here, as in drawing a crowd, not a tug on the trolley.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to attract is to draw or pull something towards you, as a magnet does iron.

blocks.note: a playing card from one of the two red suits
the core or middle of something

annotation.surface: A referee sending off a central player.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Red card' suggests football, but it is a playing card from a red suit.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a card of the red suit marked with hearts, and the core of anything, as in the heart of the city.

blocks.note: a scheduled match, as in a cup draw
the strip of cloth knotted at a shirt collar

annotation.surface: A fitting that wraps around someone's neck.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'fixture' is British for a scheduled sports match, and a cup tie is one.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a cup tie is a sports fixture, and a necktie is worn around the neck.

entries.clue: Student abandoning first scheme for making money (6)

indicatorNotes.abandoning first: abandoning the first thing means leaving the first letter behind

blocks.note: a learner = a student; its first letter L is dropped

annotation.surface: A student giving up on their original money-making plan.
annotation.walkthrough: L for learner is also familiar from the L-plates of a learner driver.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: British speech calls a profitable sideline 'a nice little earner'.

entries.clue: Wind chill turning female blue initially (6)

indicatorNotes.turning: one letter turning into another means a swap
indicatorNotes.initially: initially means at the start, so the first letter of blue

blocks.note: to chill = to make very cold
f = female, the letter that changes
first letter of blue, replacing F

annotation.surface: A cold wind turning a woman blue.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wind chill' reads as one weather term, but 'Wind' is the definition and 'chill' starts the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a breeze is a gentle wind.
